section: Chapter 9: Operations — How Storage Systems Are Updated, Upgraded, and Migrated
hook: Building a storage system takes a few years. What takes decades, and carries most of the risk?
title: Building takes years. Running takes decades.
body: A storage system is built in a few years and then run for decades. In that time every disk gets replaced, every server reboots many times, the software is upgraded thousands of times, the on-disk format changes, and eventually all the data moves to a new system. Users expect zero downtime and zero data loss through every one of those changes. That long stretch after launch is **day-2 operations**, and it is where most of the risk lives.
takeaway: Launch day is a snapshot. The system you operate is a moving target.
deeper:
**Unusual states, constantly:** Each change puts the system in a state it was not built around on launch day: mixed software versions, reduced redundancy while a server restarts, or data living in two stores at once during a migration. A system spends a surprising share of its life in one of these states.

**The toolkit:** Meta, Dropbox, Uber, Discord, GitHub, Stripe, LinkedIn, AWS and Google handle this with a small set of techniques: automated repair of failed disks, fleet-wide firmware and software updates, safe config changes, online schema changes, storage engine swaps, and large data migrations. Underneath them sit redundancy budgets, staged rollouts, cells, canaries, dual writes and rollback paths.

**The mindset:** Every operation is itself a threat to durability and availability. A repair job, an upgrade controller or a migration script deserves the same design care as the read and write path, because sooner or later it touches every byte.

quiz.q: Two teams launch equally solid storage systems. Team A designed its upgrade, migration and rollback paths up front; Team B did not. Where does Team B's risk show up, and when?
quiz.a: A year or more later, at the first format change, fleet upgrade or migration. Mixed versions, reduced redundancy and data in two places hit a system never designed for them.

mcq.q: Which phase of a storage system's life carries the most operational risk?
options: Decades of day-2 changes after launch
The initial build before launch
The first week of production traffic
The final hardware decommissioning
mcq.why: The system runs for decades while disks, servers, software, formats and eventually the whole backend change under live traffic.

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
hook: One fleet, 301,120 drives, a failure rate under 2 percent. How often does a disk die?
title: 13 dead drives a day, every day
body: Backblaze reported an **annualized failure rate** (AFR) of 1.57 percent across 301,120 data drives in 2024. Multiply it out: roughly 4,700 failed drives a year, about 13 every day, in one fleet. A hyperscaler with millions of drives replaces hundreds daily. At that scale a dead disk is not an incident to investigate. It is a background process the system must absorb without a human and without users noticing.
takeaway: At small scale a failed disk is news. At fleet scale, zero failures would be.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** Fleet size × AFR gives failures per year; divide by 365 for failures per day. 301,120 × 1.57% is about 4,700 a year, about 13 a day. A fleet of 300,000 at 1.5% lands at about 4,500 a year, roughly 12 a day.

**What it forces:** Some data is always degraded somewhere, so repair must be automated. Paging a human per disk would bury on-call in noise, so failures flow into automation plus a daily replacement ticket queue. Capacity planning has to count the drives that are always out of service waiting for a swap.

**The catch for maintenance:** Upgrades cannot assume a healthy fleet. Real failures keep arriving at the same background rate while you deliberately take servers down, so every maintenance plan must leave redundancy in reserve for them.

quiz.q: Your fleet has 300,000 drives with a 1.5 percent AFR, and on-call is paged for every disk failure. What happens, and what should change?
quiz.a: About 12 pages a day: constant noise that burns people out. Let automation repair and queue swaps, and page only on durability risk or user-visible symptoms.

mcq.q: Backblaze saw 1.57% AFR across 301,120 drives in 2024. What does that mean operationally?
options: About 13 drives fail daily, so repair must be automatic
About 13 drives fail yearly, so manual repair is fine
About 130 drives fail daily, so SMART must predict them
About 1 drive fails daily, so paging per disk is fine
mcq.why: 301,120 × 1.57% is about 4,700 a year, about 13 a day: too many for humans, so failure handling is an automated background process.

predict.q: Backblaze ran 301,120 data drives in 2024. Roughly how many failed per day?
options: About 13
About 1
About 130

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
hook: What restarts a storage server most often? Meta measured it, and the ratio is lopsided.
title: Upgrades outnumber failures 1,000 to 1
body: Meta's **Shard Manager** paper found software upgrades happen about 1,000 times more often than unplanned failures. Every kernel patch, firmware update and binary release restarts servers, and each restart briefly takes that server's data and leadership roles out of service. So the usual reason a storage server disappears is a deliberate, planned change. A system that handles crashes gracefully but treats planned restarts as an afterthought is optimizing for the rare case.

stat.label: more upgrades than unplanned failures at Meta

takeaway: Optimize for the restart you schedule, not the crash you fear.
deeper:
**Why it flips priorities:** If planned restarts outnumber crashes a thousand to one, making them invisible pays far more than shaving seconds off crash recovery. Meta designed Shard Manager largely around graceful primary handoff during planned events: before a server restarts, its primary shards move to another replica, so clients never see a leader vanish.

**The gift of notice:** A crash gives no warning. An upgrade does. The system knows which server is about to leave, so it can drain primaries, confirm no other replica of the same data is offline, and only then restart. Treating an update as a planned failure is the core move behind safe firmware rollouts, rolling upgrades and rack retirement.

**The flip side:** Every one of those frequent changes is also a chance to ship a bug. It is no surprise that change, not hardware, triggers most outages.

quiz.q: You can fund one project: 20 percent faster crash recovery, or error-free leader handoff during planned restarts. At Meta-like ratios, which improves availability more?
quiz.a: Graceful handoff. Planned restarts happen about 1,000 times more often than crashes, so making them invisible removes far more disruption than faster crash recovery.

mcq.q: What design priority follows from upgrades being about 1,000× more common than unplanned failures?
options: Make planned restarts invisible with graceful handoff
Invest mainly in faster crash detection and recovery
Stop upgrading so that restarts become rare events
Add replicas so that crashes lose less redundancy
mcq.why: Planned restarts dominate, so handing off leadership before each one removes most client-visible disruption.

predict.q: Meta compared how often servers restart for software upgrades versus unplanned failures. What ratio did it find?
options: About 1,000 upgrades per failure
About 1 upgrade per failure
About 10 failures per upgrade

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
hook: S3 in 2017 and Meta in 2021 went down for the same kind of reason. What was it?
title: Most outages start with someone pushing a change
body: Google's SRE workbook says that in Google's experience, a majority of incidents are triggered by **binary or configuration pushes**. The two most famous storage-adjacent outages of the last decade fit. On February 28, 2017, an S3 command with a wrong input removed more servers than intended. On October 4, 2021, a Meta maintenance command took down the backbone, and a bug in an audit tool failed to stop it. Neither was a disk failure or an attack. Both were operations.
takeaway: The biggest lever on reliability is not better hardware. It is safer change.
deeper:
**Three facts, one problem:** Failure is constant. Planned change is about 1,000 times more common than failure. Change causes most outages. Together they set the central operational question: how do you change a system constantly without breaking it?

**The shared shape:** In both outages a human-initiated tool executed a destructive operation at scale, and nothing inside the tool stopped it. At S3 the input was wrong and the tool removed more capacity than intended. At Meta the maintenance command was the trigger, and the check that should have blocked it had a bug.

**The answers:** Staged rollouts and canaries detect bad changes early. Cells limit how much one bad change can hurt. Guardrails in tools stop a wrong input from removing too much capacity. Destructive operations are made slow and reviewed.

**The quiet warning:** Meta's audit tool was the safety net, and the net had a hole. Safety checks need testing too.

quiz.q: A team spends its reliability budget on premium drives and extra replicas, but engineers push config straight to the whole fleet. Where will its next big incident most likely come from?
quiz.a: A binary or config push. Google finds most incidents are triggered by pushes, so staged rollout and tool guardrails buy more reliability than better hardware.

mcq.q: What did the S3 2017 and Meta 2021 outages have in common?
options: An operational command did damage at scale unchecked
A correlated firmware bug hit one drive model
A regional power failure took out several zones
A slow disk dragged down tail latency fleet-wide
mcq.why: Both were operations: a wrong-input removal command at S3, a maintenance command plus a buggy audit tool at Meta. No hardware fault.

predict.q: Google looked at what triggers most of its incidents. What came out on top?
options: Binary or configuration pushes
Hardware and disk failures
Sudden traffic spikes from users

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
hook: Your storage design passed review and is safe on launch day. Why might it be dangerous a year from now?
title: A design isn't done until you can roll it back
body: Storage design reviews usually ask whether a system is fast, durable and correct. The questions that decide its second year are different: how do we **upgrade** it, how do we **migrate** off it, and how do we **roll back**? Skip them and the system is safe on launch day and dangerous a year later. The first format change, fleet upgrade or replacement store arrives, and nobody planned for mixed versions, dual writes or undoing a bad change.
takeaway: Ask how you'll leave a system before you move into it.
deeper:
**Upgrade means compatibility:** Old and new binaries must run side by side for days, reading each other's data and messages, under a controller that never restarts too many copies of the same data at once.

**Migrate means a seam:** If data access goes through one service instead of 200 direct clients, a future backend swap changes one codebase. A data model that leans on quirks only this store supports makes every exit harder.

**Roll back means reversibility:** Every step of every change must be undoable. In practice that pushes teams toward two-phase format changes, feature flags, expand-and-contract schemas, and keeping the old system receiving writes after a cutover.

**Why ask now:** All three properties are cheap to design in and very expensive to retrofit. A store with no abstraction layer, or an on-disk format old code cannot read, can turn a routine upgrade into a year-long project.

quiz.q: A reviewer asks how you would migrate off a store you haven't built yet. The author calls the question premature. Who is right, and why?
quiz.a: The reviewer. Migration readiness, meaning an abstraction layer, compatible formats and rollback paths, costs little on paper and a lot to retrofit once hundreds of clients depend on the store.

mcq.q: Which three questions should every storage design review answer?
options: How to upgrade it, migrate off it, and roll it back
How to shard it, cache it, and compress it
How to encrypt it, audit it, and back it up
How to benchmark it, monitor it, and page on it
mcq.why: Systems that skip upgrade, migration and rollback are safe at launch and dangerous a year later, when those changes arrive.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: A disk dies at 3am. Nobody wakes up, and by morning the data is fully protected again. What ran?
title: From dead disk to full redundancy, no humans
body: When a disk dies, some data loses a copy or an erasure-coded fragment and becomes **degraded**: less redundancy than intended. **Repair** restores full redundancy before another failure lands. The loop: detect the problem, quarantine the disk and stop new writes, find the affected chunks or placement groups, prioritize those with the fewest copies left, rebuild on disks in valid failure domains, verify checksums, then file a ticket for the swap.
takeaway: Software restores safety. The drive swap only restores capacity.
deeper:
**Hidden decisions:** The loop is easy to draw, and every box hides a judgment call.
1. Detection is trivial for a dead disk and hard for one that is slow or throws occasional errors.
2. Quarantine trades wasted bandwidth on a disk that might come back against time spent degraded.
3. Finding affected data needs accurate metadata mapping disks to chunks or placement groups.
4. Rebuild targets must obey failure-domain rules, so a new copy never lands in a surviving copy's rack.

**Why verify:** Checksums confirm the new copies are correct, not faithfully duplicated corruption.

**The ordering is the point:** Software rebuilds the lost copies across the cluster long before a technician touches the dead drive. The swap is a capacity chore, not a durability emergency, so it can wait in a daily ticket queue.

quiz.q: A dead drive sits in its slot for two days before a technician swaps it. The durability dashboard stayed green the whole time. Is that a problem?
quiz.a: No. Repair already rebuilt the lost copies on other disks, restoring full redundancy. The swap only restores capacity, so a routine ticket queue is fine.

mcq.q: In the automated repair loop, which data should be rebuilt first?
options: Data with the fewest remaining copies or fragments
Data on the disk that failed most recently
Data belonging to the largest tenants
Data that was written most recently
mcq.why: Priority follows remaining redundancy: data closest to its last copy is closest to loss.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: A disk that dies outright is easy to handle. What kind of disk hurts users more?
title: Dead disks are easy. Slow disks are the trouble
body: Repair detection watches for disk errors, missed heartbeats and SMART alerts. A completely dead disk is easy to spot. A disk that is merely slow, or returns occasional errors, still answers, so it can pass simple health checks for a long time. Meanwhile it drags down every request that touches it. Many systems therefore treat a disk with rising latency as failing and **drain** it proactively, moving its data away while it still works.
takeaway: A dead disk leaves the room. A slow one stays and slows everyone.
deeper:
**Why slow beats dead:** A dead disk gets removed and its reads go elsewhere. A slow disk stays in service. Many storage reads fan out across several disks, such as the fragments of an erasure-coded stripe, so one slow disk makes every read that includes it slow. At high fan-out, the slowest participant decides the latency.

**How you find it:** An average across a node can look healthy while one disk has a terrible tail. Per-disk latency histograms expose the outlier.

**Why drain early:** Copying data off a still-readable disk is cheaper and gentler than reconstructing it after the disk dies. A direct copy reads the data once. Reconstruction reads other replicas or, with erasure coding, many fragments for each lost one. Rising latency and error counts are the cheapest failure warning you will ever get.

quiz.q: One disk in a node serves reads far slower than its peers but never returns an error. The node's average latency looks fine. Why drain that disk now?
quiz.a: Fanned-out reads, such as erasure-coded ones, wait for the slowest disk, so it slows every request touching it. Copying data off while it still reads is cheaper than rebuilding later.

mcq.q: Why do many storage systems drain a disk whose latency is rising?
options: A slow disk slows every fanned-out read touching it
Rising latency proves the disk has already lost data
Slow disks consume more repair bandwidth when dead
SMART counters stop reporting once latency rises
mcq.why: It stays in service, so reads that fan out across disks all wait on it. Draining while it's readable is also cheaper than rebuilding.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: A server stops responding. Repair could start this second. Why do good systems deliberately wait?
title: Why storage waits before repairing a lost server
body: When a server stops responding, its disks usually return within minutes after a reboot. Starting repair instantly would copy huge amounts of data for nothing and compete with user traffic. So systems wait a short **grace period** before declaring the disks lost; Ceph, for example, waits before marking an OSD 'out'. The price: every minute of waiting is a minute that data stays degraded and exposed to a second failure. After the grace period, risk-based priority takes over.
takeaway: Patience saves bandwidth; impatience saves data. Tune the grace period for both.
deeper:
**The scale of the waste:** A server with 36 drives of 20 TB, about 70 percent full, holds about 500 TB. Launching a 500 TB rebuild because a machine took five minutes to reboot is an enormous, pointless load on the network and on every source disk.

**How Ceph does it:** An OSD (object storage daemon, roughly one per disk) that stops responding is first marked down. Only after a delay is it marked out, at which point its placement groups are remapped and recovery begins.

**A tunable trade-off:** The grace period trades bandwidth efficiency against time spent degraded. Too short and every reboot triggers a flood of copying. Too long and a second failure can catch data with reduced redundancy.

**Pair it with priority:** Data already near its last copy should not wait as patiently as data missing just one copy.

quiz.q: A rack's servers all reboot for a kernel patch and return in six minutes. Your repair system started rebuilding immediately. What did that cost, and what should it do instead?
quiz.a: Massive wasted bandwidth rebuilding data that came back, competing with users. It should wait a short grace period before declaring disks lost, then repair by risk.

mcq.q: What is the main risk of making the repair grace period too long?
options: Data stays degraded and exposed to a second failure
Rebooted servers return with stale, unreadable data
Repair bandwidth is wasted on servers that come back
Placement rules are violated by the rebuilt copies
mcq.why: Waiting avoids wasted rebuilds, but the whole time data has reduced redundancy, so another failure could cause loss.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: Repair finishes fast, copy count is back to three, every dashboard is green. The data is less safe. How?
title: Rebuilt copies must still obey rack rules
body: Repair cannot drop a replacement copy on whatever disk has free space. The new copy must respect the same **failure-domain** rules as the originals: copies of the same data live in different racks, power domains or other units that fail together. So the replacement cannot land in the same rack as a surviving copy. Break the rule and the data looks fully redundant while one rack failure can still destroy it.
takeaway: Count failure domains, not copies.
deeper:
**The naive scheduler:** Optimizing only for speed, a repair scheduler picks the emptiest or nearest disk. The copy count returns to three and dashboards turn green, but two copies may now share a rack. One top-of-rack switch failure or power event takes out both. Redundancy was restored on paper and reduced in reality.

**Erasure codes too:** Each fragment of a stripe should sit in a distinct failure domain, so the stripe survives as many domain losses as it has parity. Repair has to find a target that preserves that.

**The tension with speed:** Spreading each disk's data across many other disks lets rebuild run in parallel. Failure-domain rules shrink the set of eligible targets, so placement must satisfy both goals at once. That is also why changes to placement rules deserve automated invariant checks.

quiz.q: After a disk failure, repair puts the new replica in rack 7, which already holds one of the two surviving copies. The count reads 3 of 3. What is the real protection level?
quiz.a: Against rack failure, effectively two copies. One rack 7 outage destroys two replicas at once, so the chunk is less safe than its count suggests.

mcq.q: Where may repair place a replacement copy of a chunk?
options: On a disk in a different failure domain from survivors
On the emptiest disk anywhere in the cluster
On the disk closest to the surviving source copy
On a spare disk inside a surviving copy's rack
mcq.why: Replacement copies follow the same failure-domain rules as the originals, or one rack failure can take out several copies.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: A dead server held about 500 TB. How long does the rest of the cluster need to rebuild it?
title: Rebuilding a 500 TB server: 6 days or 14 hours
body: A server with 36 drives of 20 TB, about 70 percent full, holds about 500 TB. If it dies for good and the cluster rebuilds at 1 GB/s total, that takes about 500,000 seconds, almost 6 days. At 10 GB/s it takes about 14 hours. That throughput is **repair bandwidth**, and it competes with user traffic. You get more of it by spreading the rebuild across many source and target disks.
takeaway: The rebuild window is the danger window. Parallelism is how you shrink it.
deeper:
**Why the window matters:** For those 6 days, every chunk that had a copy on the dead server runs one copy short. A second or third failure inside the window can lose data. Cutting 6 days to 14 hours shrinks that exposure roughly tenfold.

**Where 10 GB/s comes from:** Not from one disk; a single drive only writes so fast. It comes from parallelism. If the dead server's data is scattered across hundreds of disks, hundreds of sources each send a slice while hundreds of targets each receive one.

**Why no mirror partner:** With a fixed mirror partner, the whole rebuild funnels through one surviving disk and one new disk. It is slow and it hammers both. Spreading each disk's data widely is what makes fast repair possible.

**The catch:** Faster repair takes bandwidth from users. The fix is to scale repair speed with risk, not to pick one fixed rate.

quiz.q: Design A mirrors each disk to one fixed partner. Design B scatters each disk's data across hundreds of disks. A 20 TB disk dies. Which rebuilds faster, and why?
quiz.a: Design B. Hundreds of source and target disks rebuild slices in parallel, while Design A funnels everything through one surviving disk and one replacement.

mcq.q: A 500 TB server dies. What changes its rebuild from about 6 days to about 14 hours?
options: Raising total rebuild throughput from 1 to 10 GB/s
Switching from replication to RS(10,4) coding
Waiting longer before declaring the server lost
Rebuilding onto a single fixed mirror partner
mcq.why: 500 TB at 1 GB/s is about 500,000 seconds; at 10 GB/s about 14 hours. Spreading the rebuild widely supplies that throughput.

predict.q: A server holding about 500 TB dies. The cluster rebuilds at 1 GB/s total. How long until redundancy is restored?
options: Almost 6 days
About 14 hours
About 1 hour

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: Erasure coding saves disk compared with three replicas. What does it quietly cost every time a disk dies?
title: Erasure coding's hidden tax: 10× repair traffic
body: Erasure coding stores data more cheaply than replication, then charges you at repair time. With **RS(10,4)**, a Reed-Solomon code with 10 data and 4 parity fragments, rebuilding one lost fragment means reading 10 surviving fragments and decoding. Repair traffic is about 10× the data lost. With 3-way replication you copy from one surviving replica. That is why Azure Storage uses **LRC** (local reconstruction codes), which cut repair reads.

stat.label: repair reads per lost byte under RS(10,4)

takeaway: When you choose a redundancy scheme, you also choose your repair bill.
deeper:
**Scale it up:** Rebuilding a 500 TB server that held RS(10,4) data means reading on the order of 5 PB across the cluster, not 500 TB. Repair either takes far longer or eats far more network, and a whole-rack loss makes it much worse.

**Why 10:** Reed-Solomon decoding needs 10 of the stripe's 14 fragments to reconstruct a missing one. Replication needs only one intact copy.

**How LRC helps:** Local reconstruction codes add local parity computed over smaller groups of data fragments. A single lost fragment can be rebuilt from its small local group instead of the whole stripe, which substantially reduces repair reads. Azure Storage adopted LRC for exactly this operational reason.

**The lesson:** Space efficiency is paid for once. Repair cost is paid every day, on every failure, for the life of the cluster.

quiz.q: Two clusters each lose a 20 TB disk. One uses 3-way replication, the other RS(10,4). Roughly how much data does each read to repair it?
quiz.a: Replication reads about 20 TB from one surviving copy. RS(10,4) reads about 200 TB, because each lost fragment needs 10 surviving fragments decoded.

mcq.q: Why does Azure Storage use LRC instead of plain Reed-Solomon?
options: Local parity cuts the reads needed for repair
It stores data with less overhead than RS
It removes the need for failure domains
It makes erasure coding as cheap as replication
mcq.why: LRC rebuilds a lost fragment from a small local group, reducing repair reads compared with decoding across the full stripe.

predict.q: With RS(10,4) erasure coding, how much data must repair read to rebuild one lost fragment?
options: About 10× the lost data
About the same as the lost data
About 4× the lost data

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: A rack failure leaves thousands of chunks degraded. Why is fixing them in the order they broke dangerous?
title: Repair the data closest to its last copy first
body: Not all degraded data is equally at risk. A 3-replica chunk with 2 copies left can survive one more failure; with 1 copy left it can survive none. An RS(10,4) stripe missing 3 fragments has one unit of margin left. Good repair schedulers keep a **priority queue**: the fewer remaining redundancy units, the higher the priority and the more bandwidth it may use. Ceph tracks each placement group's state, such as degraded or undersized, to order recovery by risk.
takeaway: Repair by remaining margin, not by arrival order.
deeper:
**Count margin, not failures:** Think of redundancy units as the number of additional failures data can still survive. Priority should follow that margin, not the order in which failures were detected.

**The bad-day scenario:**
1. A rack fails and thousands of chunks lose one copy.
2. A second disk fails during the rebuild.
3. A small subset of chunks drops to its last copy.
A first-in, first-out queue leaves that subset behind thousands of less urgent chunks. A risk-ordered queue jumps it to the front.

**Priority buys bandwidth too:** High-risk repair should be allowed a bigger share of cluster throughput, even at some cost to user latency. Ceph's placement group states make this practical, because the system knows for every group whether it is clean, degraded or undersized.

quiz.q: Your repair queue is FIFO. A rack failure queued 40,000 chunks missing one copy; a later disk failure left 12 chunks at their last copy. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
quiz.a: The 12 last-copy chunks wait behind 40,000 low-risk ones and could be lost. Ordering the queue by remaining redundancy rebuilds them first.

mcq.q: Which chunk should a risk-aware repair scheduler rebuild first?
options: A 3-replica chunk with 1 copy left
A 3-replica chunk with 2 copies left
An RS(10,4) stripe missing 1 fragment
An RS(10,4) stripe missing 2 fragments
mcq.why: One copy left means zero margin: the next failure loses data. Each of the others can survive at least one more loss.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: Capping repair at a gentle, fixed rate keeps user latency smooth every normal day. When does it lose data?
title: A fixed low repair rate turns bad days into loss
body: Throttling repair to a fixed low rate protects user latency, and on normal days it works: repair stays quiet and nobody notices. Then a rack fails, and a second disk dies during the rebuild. Now some data sits at its last copy, and the gentle rate keeps it there for days. One more failure and it is gone. Repair speed should **scale with risk**: slow for 'one copy missing', fast and aggressive for 'last copy'.
takeaway: Latency complaints are loud. Data loss is silent until the day it isn't.
deeper:
**Why teams fall for it:** The costs are invisible most of the time. Latency complaints arrive immediately; data-loss risk is silent until it materializes. Teams tune repair against the loud signal and set up a failure for the quiet one.

**The numbers:** At 1 GB/s a 500 TB rebuild takes almost 6 days. If a fixed throttle holds repair near that rate after a second failure, some chunks sit at their last copy for days. Letting repair jump to 10 GB/s for those chunks shrinks the window to hours.

**The better design:** Wire the priority queue to bandwidth. Data missing one redundancy unit gets repaired politely in the background. Data at minimum redundancy gets repaired as fast as the cluster allows, and a brief latency hit is accepted, because the alternative is permanent loss. The dashboard to watch: how many chunks sit at their last unit of redundancy, and how fast repair is going.

quiz.q: Your team capped repair at 1 GB/s after latency complaints. A rack fails, then another disk dies mid-rebuild. What should the repair system do differently from a normal day?
quiz.a: Lift the cap for chunks at their last copy and repair them as fast as the cluster allows, accepting a brief latency hit. Low-risk chunks can stay throttled.

mcq.q: How should repair speed be set?
options: Scaled with risk: faster as redundancy runs out
Fixed low, so user latency is always protected
Fixed high, so every chunk is fixed immediately
Set by disk age, so older disks repair first
mcq.why: A fixed low rate leaves last-copy data exposed for days on bad days. Speed should rise as remaining redundancy falls.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: Every hard drive reports its own health counters for free. Why not just replace drives when they look sick?
title: SMART: the health counters drives report on themselves
body: It would be wonderful to replace every drive shortly before it dies. Drives seem to offer the data: **SMART** (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) counters for reallocated sectors, pending sectors, seek errors, temperature and more. A reallocated sector is a bad spot the drive has already remapped to a spare area. If those counters predicted failure, surprise failures would become calm, planned swaps. The open question is whether they actually predict anything.
takeaway: Free data is tempting. Test whether it predicts before you trust it.
deeper:
**What each counter means:**
1. Reallocated sectors: bad areas the drive already found and remapped.
2. Pending sectors: areas it suspects are bad but has not remapped yet.
3. Seek errors: hints of mechanical trouble positioning the head.
4. Temperature: tracked because heat is widely believed to shorten drive life.

**The tempting rule:** 'Replace any drive with more than N reallocated sectors.' Every hard drive already reports these counters, so collecting them costs nothing, and the rule assumes failures will now be caught in advance.

**The distinction to keep:** A signal can be useful when it fires without its absence proving health. Google's 2007 FAST study of a large drive population shows why SMART's silence proves nothing. That decides where it belongs in a repair pipeline: as a trigger to act, never as a reason to relax.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes lowering replication because 'we replace any drive with more than N reallocated sectors, so failures are caught early.' Which assumption should you challenge?
quiz.a: That SMART counters predict most failures. Many drives fail with clean counters, so redundancy must still cover surprise failures.

mcq.q: What does a reallocated-sector count in SMART record?
options: Bad spots the drive has remapped to spare areas
Sectors the drive suspects but has not remapped
Seek errors from head positioning problems
Writes redirected by the drive's garbage collector
mcq.why: A reallocated sector is a bad area the drive found and remapped; pending sectors are the suspected-but-not-yet-remapped ones.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: Google checked the SMART records of drives that actually failed. How many had warned anyone first?
title: Over a third of failed drives showed no SMART warning
body: Google's 2007 FAST study of a large drive population concluded that models based on **SMART parameters alone** are unlikely to be useful for predicting individual drive failures. Over 56 percent of failed drives had no counts in the four strongest SMART signals. Even using every SMART parameter, over 36 percent had zero counts on all of them. Temperature and activity were also much less correlated with failure than expected.

stat.label: of failed drives had zero SMART counts

takeaway: No threshold can catch a failure that left nothing to threshold.
deeper:
**Read the numbers carefully:** The four counters most associated with failure were silent for more than half the drives that failed. Widening the net to every SMART parameter still left more than a third with nothing to report. No tuning of thresholds could have flagged them.

**The temperature surprise:** Heat and heavy activity are commonly assumed to kill drives. In this population both were much less correlated with failure than expected, which undercuts intuitive rules like 'replace the hottest drives first'.

**Who and where:** Pinheiro, Weber and Barroso, Failure Trends in a Large Disk Drive Population, FAST 2007.

**So what:** Any storage system that relies on SMART prediction to avoid surprise failures will still be surprised, often. Redundancy and fast repair have to carry the load; prediction is a bonus on top.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches a model trained only on SMART counters that 'eliminates surprise drive failures.' Using Google's 2007 data, what limits what it can catch?
quiz.a: Over 36 percent of failed drives had zero SMART counts, so no SMART-only model can flag them. Surprise failures remain, and redundancy must handle them.

mcq.q: What did Google's 2007 FAST study find about SMART and drive failure?
options: Over 36% of failed drives had zero SMART counts
High temperature was the strongest failure signal
SMART predicted about 90% of individual failures
Only drives over five years old showed warnings
mcq.why: Many failed drives showed no SMART signal at all, and temperature correlated less than expected, so SMART alone can't predict individual failures.

predict.q: Google studied failed drives in a large population. What share had zero counts on every SMART variable?
options: Over 36 percent
About 5 percent
Under 1 percent

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
hook: A drive's SMART counters are spotless. What should that tell you about its health?
title: Use SMART to drain early, never as proof of health
body: Many drives die with a clean SMART record, so the right use is **asymmetric**. When SMART counters or error logs fire, drain the drive early and move its data while it still reads. When they stay quiet, conclude nothing: silence is not health. The storage system must survive surprise failures anyway, through redundancy and fast, risk-prioritized repair. SMART is a helpful bonus on top of that design, never its foundation.
takeaway: A warning light that fires is useful. One that stays dark proves nothing.
deeper:
**A pattern for noisy signals:** A signal can be valuable when positive and useless when negative. SMART warnings do correlate with trouble for some drives, and acting on them is cheap. Copying from a still-readable disk is faster and gentler than rebuilding its data from other replicas or fragments after it dies.

**The trap:** Letting SMART shrink your redundancy planning. A team that believed SMART caught most failures might lower replication, lengthen the repair grace period, or throttle repair harder. Over 36 percent of failed drives in Google's study showed no signal at all, so each of those choices raises real loss risk.

**The right role:** At the device level, SMART counters, media errors, reallocated sectors, temperature and per-disk latency histograms all serve one purpose: early drain of failing or slow disks. An input, not a guarantee.

quiz.q: Drive A shows rising reallocated sectors. Drive B shows zero counts everywhere. What should the storage system do with each?
quiz.a: Drain A early while it still reads. Treat B normally but assume it can still fail without warning; redundancy and repair must cover it.

mcq.q: How should a storage system treat a drive with a perfectly clean SMART record?
options: As still able to fail without warning
As healthy enough to hold a sole copy
As a candidate for a longer repair grace
As safe to exclude from scrubbing
mcq.why: Many failed drives never showed SMART signals, so a clean record is not evidence of health.

section: 9.3 Firmware and drive updates at fleet scale
hook: Three replicas, three racks, three power feeds. One update can still wipe out all three at once. How?
title: Bad firmware can hit every drive of a model at once
body: Drives, SSDs, NICs and BMCs (baseboard management controllers) all run firmware, and firmware bugs can corrupt data, collapse performance or brick devices. Updating millions of them is risky for two reasons. A bad version can hit every drive of the same model at once: a **correlated failure** that spreading replicas across racks does not help with if every rack uses that model. And some updates need a power cycle or a server reboot.
takeaway: Rack diversity means nothing if every rack runs the same bug.
deeper:
**The broken assumption:** Most redundancy math assumes independent failures: disks die one at a time for unrelated reasons, so losing every copy at once is very unlikely. Firmware breaks that. If one version corrupts data or bricks drives under some condition, every drive running it meets that condition at roughly the same time.

**Why reboots matter:** A firmware update is not a file copy. Each updated server leaves service for a while, taking its replicas and leadership roles with it. Across a fleet that adds up to a large amount of planned unavailability.

**The squeeze:** That planned downtime has to fit inside the redundancy budget while real failures keep arriving in the background, about 13 a day in a Backblaze-sized fleet.

**The defenses:** Model and firmware diversity, staged rollout, draining before update, and a strict redundancy budget.

quiz.q: A chunk's three replicas sit in different racks, but every rack uses the same SSD model on the same firmware. That version has a bug that bricks drives after a specific command. What protection does the chunk have?
quiz.a: Effectively none against that bug. The failure is correlated, so all three copies can die together. Spreading replicas across models or firmware versions is the defense.

mcq.q: Why doesn't spreading replicas across racks protect against a firmware bug?
options: Every rack can run the same model and firmware
Firmware bugs only affect drives in one rack
Racks share one BMC that pushes the firmware
Replicas are rebuilt too slowly after updates
mcq.why: The bug hits every drive on that version at once, a correlated failure that physical spreading doesn't break.

section: 9.3 Firmware and drive updates at fleet scale
hook: A firmware bug caught on five drives is cheap. Found fleet-wide, it's a disaster. What separates the two?
title: Firmware safety: mix the models, stage the rollout
body: Two practices guard against correlated firmware failure. **Diversity**: when possible, avoid putting every replica of a chunk on the same drive model or firmware version, so one bad version cannot hit every copy. **Staged rollout**: update a few drives, then a few servers, then a rack, then a cluster, watching error rates and latency at each step. Confidence grows before exposure does.
takeaway: Let exposure grow only as fast as confidence.
deeper:
**Diversity is a failure domain:** It extends placement from physical location to hardware and software identity. Drive model and firmware version become dimensions to spread across, like rack and power domain. It is not always possible, since a fleet may be dominated by one model bought in bulk. Even partial diversity helps: if a chunk's copies span two firmware versions, a bug in one leaves the other copy intact.

**Staged rollout is canarying:** Each stage is a checkpoint where error rates and latency are compared with the rest of the fleet. Both practices are widely used and described in general terms by many operators.

**The firmware wrinkle:** Some bugs surface only under particular workloads or after time passes. A quick health check after each stage misses them. Bake time at every stage gives slow bugs a chance to show up while few drives are exposed.

quiz.q: Your fleet is 90 percent one SSD model. New firmware fixes a performance issue. How do you roll it out without risking correlated loss?
quiz.a: Stage it: a few drives, a few servers, a rack, a cluster, baking and comparing errors and latency at each step. Where possible, keep each chunk's replicas on different firmware versions.

mcq.q: What does spreading replicas across firmware versions protect against?
options: One bad version corrupting every copy of a chunk
A single rack losing power during an update
Slow disks inflating erasure-coded read latency
Operators pushing firmware to the wrong cluster
mcq.why: If a chunk's copies span firmware versions, a bug in one version leaves the copies on the other version intact.

section: 9.3 Firmware and drive updates at fleet scale
hook: A stripe can survive 4 lost fragments. Why should maintenance take at most 1 or 2 of them offline?
title: Treat every update as a planned failure, within budget
body: Maintenance spends redundancy on purpose, so it needs a spending limit. First, **drain before update**: treat it like a planned failure by moving primaries away, updating, verifying, then returning the device to service. Second, respect the **redundancy budget**: never take more offline than the system can lose while still meeting its durability target. If a stripe survives 4 losses, allow at most 1 to 2 fragments offline for maintenance. Real failures keep happening meanwhile.
takeaway: Maintenance may borrow redundancy. It must never spend the failure reserve.
deeper:
**Why drain first:** If a server holds shard primaries or leader roles, moving them to other replicas before the restart means no client request lands on a machine mid-reboot. After the update, verification (device back, firmware version correct, error rates normal) happens before it takes traffic again.

**The budget, concretely:** While a server is offline, every stripe with a fragment on it has one less unit of margin. RS(10,4) tolerates 4 lost fragments. Taking at most 1 to 2 offline for maintenance leaves 2 to 3 units for real failures.

**Why keep a reserve:** Unplanned failures do not pause for your maintenance window. A Backblaze-sized fleet loses about 13 drives a day regardless.

**Where it reappears:** Rolling software upgrades obey the same budget: the controller never restarts two servers holding copies of the same data at once.

quiz.q: An RS(10,4) cluster needs a firmware update. An engineer wants to take 4 fragments of each stripe offline at once to finish faster. What's wrong?
quiz.a: It spends the whole loss budget on planned work. Any real failure during the update, and they keep coming, would lose data. Keep 1 to 2 offline at most.

mcq.q: A stripe tolerates 4 lost fragments. How many should maintenance take offline at once?
options: At most 1 to 2, keeping margin for failures
Up to 4, since the stripe survives that many
None; maintenance must wait for a full drain
Up to 3, leaving a single fragment spare
mcq.why: Real failures continue during maintenance, so part of the redundancy budget must stay reserved for them.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: Mid-upgrade, half your servers run v2 and half run v1, for days. Then v2 misbehaves. Can you roll back?
title: Rolling upgrades: old and new code must read each other
body: During a **rolling upgrade**, servers restart a few at a time on the new version while the rest keep serving, so old and new versions run side by side, sometimes for days. New code must read data and messages written by old code: backward compatibility. For rollback, old code must read what new code wrote: forward compatibility. Miss the first and the upgrade breaks midway. Miss the second and rollback fails exactly when you need it.
takeaway: Storage data outlives the binary that wrote it.
deeper:
**Why storage is harder:** A stateless web server can be replaced and its old version forgotten. A storage server writes bytes to disk and messages to replicas, and those bytes will be read by whatever version runs later, possibly an older one after a rollback.

**Two ways it breaks:**
1. A new version writes records in a new format. An old-version replica receives a replication message it cannot parse, and the mixed cluster breaks mid-upgrade.
2. The new version has a bug and you roll back. The old binary finds data on disk it cannot read, and rollback fails.

**Not an edge case:** Large fleets upgrade in waves with bake time in between, so the mixed-version state is normal for a big share of a system's life. Two-way compatibility sits alongside graceful leader handoff and a redundancy budget as the requirements for zero-downtime upgrades.

quiz.q: Version 5 of your storage server writes a new record format that v4 can't parse. You're 40 percent through a rolling upgrade when v5 shows a bug. What two things go wrong?
quiz.a: During the upgrade, v4 replicas choke on v5's replication messages. On rollback, v4 binaries find v5-format data on disk they can't read.

mcq.q: Why does a storage rolling upgrade need forward compatibility?
options: So old code can read data new code wrote, for rollback
So new code can read data that old code wrote
So both versions can share one on-disk index
So upgraded servers can skip leadership handoff
mcq.why: If the new version misbehaves, rolling back puts old binaries in front of data the new version already wrote.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: To the rest of the cluster, restarting a Raft leader looks exactly like a crash. How do you avoid that?
title: Move leadership away before you restart the leader
body: Kill a leader abruptly and clients get errors while its group elects a replacement. So before restarting a server that is a shard primary or a **Raft leader**, the replica coordinating writes for its group, a rolling upgrade first moves that leadership to another replica. This is **graceful handoff**. Clients keep talking to a healthy leader and never see one vanish mid-request. Meta's Shard Manager was designed largely for this during planned events.
takeaway: If you know a leader is leaving, never make the cluster discover it.
deeper:
**Without handoff:** Restarting a leader looks like a crash. Clients get errors or timeouts. Replicas must notice the leader is gone, often via missed heartbeats, then hold an election or failover, and only then resume writes. That gap may last seconds, and in a large rolling upgrade it happens to every leader in the fleet.

**With handoff:**
1. The current leader stops accepting new writes.
2. It makes sure a successor is caught up.
3. It hands over leadership and redirects clients.
Because the restart is known in advance, this can happen with no failed requests.

**Why Meta built for it:** Shard Manager (SOSP 2021) pairs this with the finding that upgrades are about 1,000 times more common than unplanned failures. If planned restarts dominate, making them invisible is one of the most valuable things a shard manager can do.

quiz.q: A rolling upgrade restarts 2,000 Raft leaders abruptly, and each restart causes a few seconds of write errors for its group. What single change removes most of that, and why can it work?
quiz.a: Transfer leadership to a caught-up replica before each restart. The restart is planned, so the handoff finishes before the process stops, leaving no failed requests.

mcq.q: What does graceful handoff do before a leader restarts?
options: Transfers leadership to a caught-up replica
Pauses all client writes until it returns
Triggers an election after missed heartbeats
Copies the leader's disk to a spare server
mcq.why: Moving leadership first lets clients keep writing to a healthy leader, instead of waiting through crash detection and an election.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: Your upgrade restarts 5 percent of servers at a time, in alphabetical order. Why might that lose data?
title: Never restart two holders of the same data at once
body: Every restart in a rolling upgrade temporarily removes that server's replicas. So the upgrade controller must never restart two servers holding copies of the same data at the same time; otherwise some data drops to a single copy, or goes unavailable, while they reboot. That is the **durability budget** applied to upgrades. A good controller understands data placement, not just server lists, and picks each batch so no piece of data loses too many copies at once.
takeaway: Batch restarts by data placement, not by hostname.
deeper:
**The naive version:** Restart 5 percent of servers at a time, picked alphabetically or by rack. That batch can easily include two servers sharing replicas of the same chunks. Add a real disk failure during the window and those chunks may lose their last copy.

**The placement-aware version:** For each candidate batch, the controller asks: after these servers go down, does every chunk still have enough copies or fragments to meet its durability target, with margin left for unplanned failures? Only batches that pass get restarted.

**Why layout helps:** If data is placed so any single rack or cell can go down without violating redundancy, upgrade batches can simply follow those boundaries.

**The three pillars:** Zero-downtime upgrades need version compatibility in both directions, graceful leader handoff, and this redundancy budget for maintenance.

quiz.q: A chunk's three replicas live on db-104, db-219 and db-377. Your upgrade batch contains db-104 and db-219, and db-377's disk fails mid-batch. What happened, and what prevents it?
quiz.a: All three copies are offline or gone at once, so the chunk is unavailable or lost. A placement-aware controller never batches two holders of the same data.

mcq.q: What must an upgrade controller know to respect the durability budget?
options: Which servers hold copies of the same data
Which servers have the newest hardware
Which servers currently serve the most traffic
Which servers were upgraded most recently
mcq.why: Restarting two holders of the same data together can drop it to one copy or make it unavailable.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: You need a new on-disk format, and rollback must stay safe at every step. What do you deploy first?
title: Ship the reader first, flip the writer later
body: Change a storage format in two phases. First, ship code that can read the new format but still writes the old one, and roll it out everywhere. Second, once every server runs it, flip a **feature flag**, a runtime switch that needs no new deploy, to start writing the new format. Every server could already read both formats before anything wrote the new one, so rolling back the binary is safe at every step.
takeaway: Separate 'able to handle the new thing' from 'producing the new thing'.
deeper:
**Walk the failure cases:**
1. During phase one nothing writes the new format. Roll back the binary and the old code sees only old-format data.
2. When the flag flips, every server already reads the new format, so no server receives data it cannot parse.
3. If the new format causes trouble, flip the flag back. Servers resume writing the old format and can still read what was written in the new one.

**The unsafe shortcut:** One binary that both reads and writes the new format fails twice. Mid-upgrade, new servers write data old servers cannot read. On rollback, old binaries face new-format data on disk.

**The same shape everywhere:** Expand-and-contract schema changes add a column before anything depends on it. Large migrations dual-write before switching reads. Each keeps every step reversible.

quiz.q: A teammate wants one release that both reads and writes a new format, to save a deploy cycle. What breaks during the rolling upgrade, and what breaks on rollback?
quiz.a: Mid-upgrade, old servers receive new-format data they can't parse. On rollback, old binaries meet new-format data on disk. Shipping the reader first avoids both.

mcq.q: In a two-phase format change, when do servers start writing the new format?
options: After every server can read it, via a flag flip
As soon as the first upgraded server restarts
After the old format has been deleted from disk
Before the reader code is deployed anywhere
mcq.why: Writing starts only once all servers can read the new format, so no server meets data it can't parse and rollback stays safe.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: Error rates doubled an hour after the deploy. Was it the new build, or just the evening traffic peak?
title: Canarying: a small, timed test against a control
body: Error rates move for reasons that have nothing to do with your change, and **canarying** separates the two. Google's SRE workbook defines it as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation. A small canary population runs the new version while a control population runs the old one, and you compare errors, latency and CPU to decide go or no-go. The workbook notes you do not need a large canary to catch critical problems.
takeaway: Compare against a control, not against yesterday.
deeper:
**Why a control group:** Traffic, load and error rates shift constantly with time of day and with events elsewhere. Comparing canary and control at the same moment, under the same conditions, isolates the effect of the new version. Comparing the canary with yesterday's graph does not.

**Sizing is judgment:** Severe bugs show up quickly even in a small population, so a small canary catches critical problems. But the right size depends on traffic volume, time of day and which metrics you rely on. A canary that gets little traffic, or runs through a quiet period, may never exercise the broken path.

**Time-limited matters:** The canary runs for a set evaluation period, then proceeds or rolls back. It is a decision procedure, not a permanent split.

**It generalizes:** Shifting reads gradually during a data migration is canarying applied to data.

quiz.q: Your canary shows 20 percent higher p99 latency than yesterday. The control population shows the same 20 percent rise. Go or no-go, and why?
quiz.a: Probably go, pending other metrics. Canary and control rose together, so the cause is something they share, like traffic, not the new version.

mcq.q: Why does canarying compare against a control population?
options: To separate the change's effect from normal fluctuation
To give the new version twice as much traffic
To avoid needing any rollback mechanism
To test the new version on synthetic traffic
mcq.why: Canary and control run at the same time under the same conditions, so differences reflect the change, not time-of-day shifts.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: Your storage canary is green on errors and latency. It may still be quietly damaging data. How would you know?
title: Storage canaries must watch the slow, silent metrics
body: A storage bug can corrupt data silently for days before any request fails. So storage canaries cannot rely only on error rate and latency. They must also watch signals that move slowly: **checksum mismatches**, compaction backlog, disk space growth and replication lag. These expose data written wrongly, background work falling behind, or leaking space, long before a user sees an error. Slow signals need time, so storage canaries also need longer bake times.
takeaway: Requests fail loudly. Storage fails quietly, then all at once.
deeper:
**What each metric catches:**
1. Checksum mismatches: data read back does not match what was written, the most direct sign of corruption.
2. Compaction backlog: in LSM-tree engines, background merging falls behind. A version that compacts less efficiently can look fine for hours, then stall writes days later.
3. Disk space growth: leaks, failed deletes, or writing more than intended.
4. Replication lag: replicas falling behind the primary, which erodes durability and failover readiness without failing a single request.

**The design consequence:** A storage canary that runs twenty minutes and checks only error rates would pass many dangerous changes. Storage rollouts bake longer at each wave and compare these slow metrics between canary and control.

**The underlying asymmetry:** Availability problems are loud. Durability problems are silent until data is gone. Canary analysis has to look for the silent kind on purpose.

quiz.q: A new storage build passes a 20-minute canary with flat error rates. Three days after full rollout, compaction backlog stalls writes fleet-wide. What should the canary have checked?
quiz.a: Slow storage signals, such as compaction backlog, replication lag, disk growth and checksum mismatches, compared against control over a longer bake before widening the rollout.

mcq.q: Which canary metric most directly reveals silent data corruption?
options: Checksum mismatches
Request error rate
CPU utilization
p50 read latency
mcq.why: A checksum mismatch means data read back differs from what was written, even while every request still succeeds.

predict.q: A new storage build passes a 20-minute canary with zero request errors. Which signal is most likely to expose a hidden bug?
options: Checksum mismatches over days
CPU usage in the first minute
HTTP error rate at 20 minutes

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: A bad change will slip through eventually. How do you decide in advance how many users it can hurt?
title: Cells: with 10 cells, one failure hits only 10%
body: Every change can go wrong, so what matters is its **blast radius**: how many users a bad change can hurt. Storage systems shrink it with **cells**. AWS describes a cell-based architecture as multiple isolated instances of a workload, with a thin cell router in front that routes by a partition key such as customer ID. With 10 cells serving 100 requests, a failure in one cell leaves 90 percent unaffected. Changes deploy compartment by compartment.

stat.label: of requests unaffected when 1 of 10 cells fails

takeaway: Canaries catch problems early. Cells contain the ones canaries miss.
deeper:
**Isolated is the key word:** Each cell has its own servers, storage and, ideally, its own dependencies. A bug, overload or bad config in one cell does not spread. The router is deliberately thin, because it is the one shared component and must rarely fail.

**Deploys change shape:** Instead of rolling a version across one big fleet, you roll it cell by cell. The first cell becomes a production canary with a hard wall around it.

**Why you want both:** A canary is a small, time-limited deployment that detects whether a change is bad by comparing it with a control. A cell is an isolated slice that limits how many users a bad change or failure can hurt. Detection without containment lets a subtle bug reach everyone. Containment without detection lets it roll from cell to cell until someone notices.

quiz.q: Your storage service is one big shared fleet with excellent canaries. A bug that only shows after a week slips past them. What would cells have changed?
quiz.a: The bug would have hit one cell's customers before spreading further, not everyone at once. Cells bound the damage of problems that detection misses.

mcq.q: What is the difference between a canary and a cell?
options: A canary detects bad changes; a cell limits their reach
A canary limits reach; a cell detects bad changes
A canary is one server; a cell is one datacenter
A canary is for config; a cell is for binaries
mcq.why: Canaries compare new against control to catch problems. Cells are isolated slices that cap how many users any failure can hurt.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: Most teams run a critical config store as one big database. For EBS, AWS went the opposite way. Why?
title: Physalia: millions of tiny databases for EBS
body: If one big configuration store sits behind every EBS volume, one bad change or failure in it reaches every volume at once. AWS's EBS control plane store, **Physalia** (NSDI 2020), avoids that by running 'millions of tiny databases', each holding only the configuration keys a particular client needs. Each is placed using knowledge of datacenter topology, so it is available where its client is. A failure or bad change affects a tiny slice.
takeaway: Shrink the unit of failure until one failure barely matters.
deeper:
**The context:** EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides network block volumes, and its control plane holds configuration that volumes need. As one large system, a failure or bad deployment there could affect vast numbers of volumes together.

**The inversion:** Rather than one big, highly available database, Physalia builds many very small ones, each scoped to what one client needs. The blast radius of any single failure is the set of clients using that tiny database, which by design is small. It is cell-based architecture taken to an extreme.

**Why topology matters:** Each tiny database is placed near its client in terms of datacenter layout. A network partition that isolates part of the datacenter tends to keep a client together with its configuration, so the client can still reach what it needs.

**The bigger pattern:** AWS treats failure isolation as a design property, not an afterthought.

quiz.q: A control plane keeps config for a million clients in one replicated database, and a bad change corrupts it. How would the same change play out under Physalia's design?
quiz.a: In the single database, every client is hit at once. With millions of tiny databases, each holding one client's keys, the same bad change reaches only a tiny slice.

mcq.q: How does Physalia limit the blast radius of failures in the EBS control plane?
options: Millions of tiny databases, each for one client's keys
One large database replicated across every region
A central cache that serves config if storage fails
Nightly snapshots that restore config after errors
mcq.why: Each tiny database holds only what one client needs and sits near it, so any failure touches a tiny slice.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: After a mistyped command took down S3 in 2017, AWS didn't just fix the tool. What else did it rebuild?
title: What AWS changed after the 2017 S3 outage
body: On February 28, 2017, an S3 command with a wrong input removed more servers than intended. AWS's fixes came in three parts. It changed the removal tool to take capacity away more slowly, with safeguards against dropping below **minimum capacity**. It audited other operational tools for the same risk. And it reprioritized partitioning the index subsystem into smaller **cells**, to reduce blast radius and speed recovery. The tool fix was local; the cells were structural.
takeaway: A system that never restarts has an untested recovery path.
deeper:
**The second lesson:** The index and placement subsystems had not been fully restarted in the larger regions for many years, and restarting them took longer than expected. A system that never restarts never tests its recovery path, so nobody knows how long a full restart takes until one is forced.

**Cells help twice:** Smaller cells limit how much capacity one mistaken command can touch, and each cell is smaller, so it restarts faster.

**The copyable part:** Removing capacity slowly gives humans and monitoring time to notice a mistake before it spreads. A hard floor on minimum capacity means even a wrong input cannot take the system below what it needs to function.

**Where it echoes:** The same remediation works as a guardrail for config tools, as a rule for datacenter decommissioning, and as a template for any tool that removes capacity.

quiz.q: Your metadata service hasn't had a full restart in six years and has grown tenfold. Based on S3's 2017 outage, why is that a risk?
quiz.a: Full-restart recovery has never been tested at its current size, so it may take far longer than expected. Smaller cells and restart testing keep recovery fast.

mcq.q: Which change did AWS make to its capacity-removal tool after the 2017 S3 outage?
options: Remove capacity slowly, never below a minimum
Require a full index restart before removal
Remove capacity only during off-peak hours
Replace the tool with a manual console
mcq.why: AWS made the tool slower with safeguards against going below minimum capacity, so a wrong input can't remove too much at once.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: A new build is ready. In what order should it reach the world, and what decides when it moves on?
title: Deploy in waves: one box, one cell, one region, then all
body: Push a build to the whole fleet at once and a bug reaches everyone together. A safe pipeline widens in waves instead: one box in one cell, then one cell in one zone, then more cells in one region, then the remaining regions one at a time. Between waves comes **bake time**: waiting while metrics are watched. If metrics look wrong at any checkpoint, the pipeline triggers **automatic rollback**.
takeaway: Bake time is the protection. Skip it and the waves are decoration.
deeper:
**How the pieces combine:** Canarying supplies the evaluation at each step: new versus old on errors and latency, plus slow storage signals like checksum mismatches and replication lag. Cells supply containment: each wave is bounded by cell, zone and region, so a bad build that slips past one checkpoint still hurts a limited set of users. Regions go one at a time, so even the last wave never exposes everyone at once.

**Why bake time:** Slow storage bugs need time to surface. A pipeline that races through its waves offers little protection.

**Why automatic rollback:** Humans are slow and, during incidents, tired. If a metric crosses a threshold during bake, the pipeline should revert without waiting for someone to decide.

**The fine print:** Rollback is only safe if versions are compatible in both directions and format changes shipped reader-first.

quiz.q: A pipeline has four waves but bakes only two minutes each, so a full rollout takes ten minutes. A storage bug causes disk-space growth that shows after six hours. How much of the fleet does it reach?
quiz.a: All of it. Every wave passed before the symptom appeared. Bake times must be long enough for slow storage signals to show up.

mcq.q: What should a deployment pipeline do when metrics look wrong during bake time?
options: Roll back automatically without waiting
Proceed and page an engineer to decide
Skip ahead to the final wave to finish
Extend the bake and keep the build live
mcq.why: Humans are slow and tired in incidents; automatic rollback limits a bad build to the current wave.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
hook: AWS, Google and Meta each solved a different piece of safe deployment. What are the three pieces?
title: Detect, contain, hide: deployment safety as design
body: Changing a system constantly without users noticing takes three separate capabilities. AWS (cells, and Physalia in 2020), Google (canarying in its SRE workbook) and Meta (Shard Manager, 2021) all treat them as design properties, not processes bolted on later. **Canaries** detect a bad change early by comparing it with a control. **Cells** limit the damage any single change can do. **Graceful handoff** makes the restarts themselves invisible to clients.
takeaway: Detection, containment and invisible restarts: each covers a gap the others leave.
deeper:
**Why one isn't enough:** Canaries alone miss bugs too rare or slow to show up in a small canary, and a change that passes still reaches everyone. Cells alone let a bad change roll from cell to cell until someone notices. Graceful handoff solves a different problem: even a perfect build causes disruption if deploying it means abruptly killing leaders across the fleet.

**Why 'design property':** These shape architecture. You cannot add cells to a system whose data and dependencies are all shared without major rework. You cannot hand off gracefully without a shard manager or consensus protocol that supports leadership transfer. You cannot canary meaningfully without metrics comparable between canary and control.

**The payoff:** Teams that answered 'how do we upgrade it and roll it back?' at design time are the ones whose constant changes rarely become outages.

quiz.q: A team has great canaries and cells, yet every deploy still causes a burst of client errors, even for good builds. Which piece is missing?
quiz.a: Graceful handoff. Restarting leaders abruptly looks like a crash to clients; moving leadership before each restart makes deploys invisible.

mcq.q: In the detect, contain, hide split, what does graceful handoff contribute?
options: It makes planned restarts invisible to clients
It detects bad builds by comparing to a control
It limits how many users a bad change can hurt
It rolls back automatically when metrics fail
mcq.why: Canaries detect, cells contain, and handoff hides restarts by moving leadership before a server goes down.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
hook: No new code shipped. One value in a file changed. How does that take down a fleet?
title: Config is 'just data' until it takes you down
body: A **config change** alters behavior without new code: a flag, a limit, a routing table, a placement rule, a quota. It feels safe because it is 'just data'. It is not. Google explicitly lists configuration pushes, next to binary pushes, as the main incident triggers. The Meta 2021 outage started with a maintenance command, and the S3 2017 outage with a mistyped command parameter. One wrong value can change how an entire fleet routes traffic or places data.
takeaway: Anything that changes behavior is code, whatever file it lives in.
deeper:
**Why config bites:**
1. It often skips the review, testing and staged rollout code gets, precisely because it looks harmless.
2. It takes effect quickly and often fleet-wide, since the point is to change behavior without a redeploy.
3. It is as powerful as code: a placement rule decides where every replica lives, a quota decides who can write, a routing table decides where every request goes.

**The outages:** Neither S3 nor Meta involved a new binary. Both involved an operator-supplied instruction executed at scale.

**Storage makes it worse:** Config mistakes can hurt durability, not just availability. A bad placement rule might put several replicas in one rack. The system keeps working and looks healthy until that rack fails, and then the data is gone.

quiz.q: A placement-rule change passes review because the diff is two lines. Weeks later a rack fails and some chunks lose every copy. How did a harmless-looking config cause data loss?
quiz.a: The rule put multiple replicas in the same rack. Config is as powerful as code, and durability damage stays invisible until a failure exposes it.

mcq.q: Why is a config push often riskier than it looks?
options: It skips code's safeguards but takes effect fleet-wide
It needs a server reboot before it takes effect
It can only change cosmetic behavior like logging
It is rolled out one cell at a time by default
mcq.why: Config feels like data, so it often bypasses review and staging, yet it can change routing, placement or capacity everywhere at once.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
hook: A bad config value can be live everywhere in seconds. Which three habits make it as safe as a code deploy?
title: Treat config like code: reviewed, staged, reversible
body: Experienced storage teams give config the same safety net as binaries, through three rules. **Config is code**: it lives in version control and is reviewed, tested and validated before rollout. It goes through the **same staged rollout** as binaries: canary, cells, waves, with bake time between. And it keeps a **fast rollback**: the last known good config sits ready to push, so a bad change is reverted in moments.
takeaway: You can't quickly restore a state you never recorded.
deeper:
**Version control:** It records who changed what, when and why, and it makes the last known good config trivially retrievable. Review catches the typo or wrong number the author missed. Validation runs the new config through checks before any production system sees it.

**Staging matters most:** A config pushed to every server at once has unlimited blast radius. The same config pushed to one cell, then more cells, then regions, with metric comparison at each step, turns a potential global outage into a contained one. Config changes need the same pipeline as code.

**Rollback in one action:** Config problems often show up immediately. If the last known good version is ready to push, recovery is a single action instead of a scramble to remember the previous values.

quiz.q: At 2am a quota change breaks writes for every tenant. Nobody remembers the old value, and the change wasn't in version control. Which three practices would have shrunk this incident?
quiz.a: Version-controlled, reviewed config; staged rollout so only one cell broke first; and the last known good config ready to push back instantly.

mcq.q: Which rule most limits a bad config value's blast radius?
options: Staged rollout through canary, cells and waves
Keeping the config file small and readable
Letting only senior engineers edit config
Applying config changes during off-peak hours
mcq.why: A config pushed everywhere at once hits everyone; staging exposes one cell first and compares metrics before widening.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
hook: A reviewer approves a placement-rule diff. Two fragments now share a rack. Why didn't the reviewer see it?
title: Guardrails and invariants: let programs say no
body: Humans reviewing a config diff miss subtle violations, so two rules move safety into software. **Guardrails** in tools: a command that removes capacity must refuse to remove more than a safe fraction, and must move slowly, as in the S3 remediation. **Invariant validation**: express safety rules as properties a program checks before rollout, such as 'this placement rule leaves every stripe with at least N fragments in distinct racks'. Checked by a program, not by eye.
takeaway: When a mistake is catastrophic, make the system refuse instead of trusting care.
deeper:
**Guardrails beat good intentions:** Safety should not depend on the operator typing the right value. A capacity-removal command with a hard ceiling and a slow execution rate makes a wrong input survivable. Ask it to remove a whole region and it refuses, or proceeds slowly enough for monitoring to catch it. AWS added exactly these safeguards after the 2017 S3 outage.

**Invariants beat eyeballs:** A placement change can look reasonable in review yet, combined with the current rack layout, leave some stripes with two fragments in one rack. The only reliable way to know is to evaluate the rule against the real topology and data layout and check every stripe.

**The shared principle:** Use actual metadata, not assumptions. The same rule governs decommissioning: a program confirms nothing still has its only copy on hardware about to be wiped.

quiz.q: An operator runs a capacity-removal command meant for 5 hosts but types 500. What should a well-built tool do, and why?
quiz.a: Refuse, or proceed slowly under a hard ceiling that never drops capacity below minimum. Guardrails make a wrong input survivable, as in AWS's post-2017 S3 fix.

mcq.q: Why should a placement rule be validated by a program rather than human review?
options: A program can check the rule against every stripe
Programs understand intent better than reviewers
Human review slows config pushes down too much
Placement rules are too long for humans to read
mcq.why: Subtle violations depend on the real topology; only checking every stripe against the rule reliably catches them.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
hook: Mid-outage, the fix is ready and every minute counts. Should it skip the staged pipeline?
title: Emergency pushes still need staging, just faster
body: Letting 'emergency' config pushes skip the staged pipeline sounds reasonable: you want the fix out now. But emergencies are exactly when people are tired, rushed and most likely to err. A hasty fix pushed everywhere at once can turn one outage into a bigger one. The better design keeps the **fast path staged**, only with shorter bake times. Containment and detection stay; they just run faster.
takeaway: Urgency doesn't make a bad push less bad. Keep the stages, shorten the bake.
deeper:
**When errors peak:** On a normal day engineers are rested, changes are planned and reviewers have time. During an incident, the person pushing the fix may have been awake for hours, is under pressure from stakeholders, and has incomplete information about the cause. That is when a typo or a wrong assumption is most likely, and a pipeline bypass removes the very safeguards that would catch it.

**What staging still gives you:** The emergency fix goes to one cell first, gets compared against metrics, and can roll back automatically. Shorter bake times keep it fast enough. The cost is minutes; the benefit is that a wrong fix damages one cell instead of everything.

**The general rule:** Wide-reaching or irreversible actions stay slow and guarded. An urgent situation does not make the consequences of a bad push any smaller.
