quiz.a: Change: current versions, configs per cell and recent deploys. Most incidents follow a binary or config push, so a matching change is the likeliest cause.

mcq.q: Which signal level is the most important dashboard for durability risk?
options: Data: degraded chunks and repair queue
Service: request rate and error rate
Node: CPU and NIC saturation
Capacity: days until full per cluster
mcq.why: Data-level signals like chunks at minimum redundancy and repair rate directly measure how close the system is to losing data.

section: 9.10 Observability for storage
hook: Your storage node's average latency is a healthy 5 ms. How bad could its slowest requests be?
title: A 5 ms average can hide a 2-second p99.9
body: An average latency of 5 ms can hide a p99.9 of 2 seconds: one request in a thousand takes 2 seconds while the average still looks healthy. At high fan-out, where one user request touches many disks or servers, the slowest participant decides user latency. So record full latency **histograms** per disk and per node. That is how you find the one slow disk that makes every erasure-coded read touching it slow.

stat.label: p99.9 latency hiding behind a 5 ms average

takeaway: Averages describe no actual request. Histograms describe all of them.
deeper:
**How averages lie:** A slow disk might add hundreds of milliseconds to a small fraction of reads, barely moving the node's average, yet every request that includes that disk suffers.

**Fan-out amplifies it:** An erasure-coded read needs fragments from several disks at once. The more disks a read touches, the likelier it is that one of them is the slow one. The tail of one component becomes the typical experience for users.

**Per disk, not just per node:** Histograms keep the whole distribution, so p99 and p99.9 are visible and individual disks can be compared. Aggregating only per node or cluster hides the specific outlier. Once found, the slow disk can be drained proactively.

**Same rule upstairs:** Service-level latency should be tracked at p50, p99 and p99.9 per tenant and operation, never as one average.

quiz.q: A node's average read latency is steady at 5 ms, but users of erasure-coded objects report multi-second stalls. What's likely happening, and how do you find it?
quiz.a: One slow disk: EC reads that touch it wait on its tail, which barely moves the average. Per-disk latency histograms reveal which disk to drain.

mcq.q: Why keep latency histograms per disk rather than one average per node?
options: They expose the one slow disk that fan-out reads wait on
They use less storage than keeping node averages
They make the node's average latency more accurate
They replace the need for SMART monitoring
mcq.why: An average hides tails; at high fan-out one slow disk slows every read touching it, and only per-disk histograms pinpoint it.

predict.q: A storage node's average latency is a healthy 5 ms. Can its p99.9 still be as bad as 2 seconds?
options: Yes, the average can hide it
No, p99.9 stays within about 2× the average
No, p99.9 stays within about 10× the average

section: 9.10 Observability for storage
hook: When availability fails, users complain within minutes. When durability fails, who tells you?
title: Durability problems are silent until data is gone
body: Availability problems are loud: users see errors and complain. Durability problems are silent until data is gone. So storage teams must watch durability directly. The dashboard that matters most asks: how many chunks are at their last unit of redundancy right now, and how fast is repair going? **Continuous scrubbing**, background reading and checksum verification of stored data, finds silent corruption before a later failure destroys the only good copy.
takeaway: Users report outages. Nobody reports the corrupt copy they never read.
deeper:
**The asymmetry:** Monitor only what users feel and you will see outages but miss the slow build-up that causes data loss: more chunks at minimum redundancy, repair falling behind, corrupted copies nobody has read in months. All of it is invisible until one more failure turns risk into loss.

**The key number:** Chunks at their last unit of redundancy is the most direct measure of how close the system is to losing data. Paired with repair rate, it tells you whether that risk is shrinking or growing. It is also what to alert on, alongside user-visible symptoms.

**Why scrubbing:** Repair reacts to known failures, like a dead disk. Silent corruption, a disk returning wrong data without reporting an error, is not a known failure until someone reads the data and checks it. Scrubbing reads everything periodically and verifies checksums, so a bad copy is repaired while good copies still exist.

quiz.q: A chunk has three replicas. One silently corrupted months ago and nobody read it. Today a disk holding a second replica dies. How could scrubbing have prevented the danger you're now in?
quiz.a: Scrubbing would have caught the corrupt copy by checksum and repaired it from a good one. Now only one good copy remains, one failure from loss.

mcq.q: What does continuous scrubbing find that repair alone does not?
options: Silent corruption no one has read yet
Disks that stopped answering heartbeats
Servers that rebooted within the grace period
Chunks placed in the same rack by mistake
mcq.why: Repair reacts to known failures; scrubbing reads data and checks checksums to find corruption while good copies still exist.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
hook: At 3am the alert says 'repair queue growing'. Where should the on-call engineer's next click take them?
title: Good runbooks are short, tested, and become automation
body: An alert without a procedure leaves the on-call engineer improvising. That procedure is a **runbook**: documented steps for a known situation such as 'disk failed', 'node unreachable', 'repair queue growing' or 'cluster 85 percent full'. Good runbooks are short, tested, and linked from the alert itself, so nobody searches a wiki mid-incident. The best ones are gradually turned into automation, because a program runs a proven procedure faster and more consistently than a person.
takeaway: A mature runbook is a program written in English. Compile it.
deeper:
**Each property stops a failure mode:**
1. Short, because someone responding under pressure will skip or misread a long document.
2. Tested, because an unexecuted runbook may hold wrong commands or stale steps, and an incident is the worst time to find out.
3. Linked from the alert, because every minute spent finding docs is a minute the system stays broken.

**The lifecycle:** A new kind of problem is handled by humans, who write down what worked. Repeated use refines it until it is precise. At that point, translating it to code removes human error and delay.

**Scale forces it:** A Backblaze-sized fleet loses about 13 disks a day, far too many for a person to follow a manual procedure each time. Well-understood events become fully automatic; novel failures stay human-led, with a runbook and an incident process.

quiz.q: Your team has run the same 'disk failed' runbook by hand about a dozen times a day for a year, unchanged for months. What should happen to it, and why?
quiz.a: Automate it. It is precise and proven, and at that frequency a program runs it faster and without human error. Keep humans for novel failures.

mcq.q: Which trait makes a runbook ready to become automation?
options: It is precise, proven and used often
It is long enough to cover every case
It is owned by a single senior engineer
It is stored next to the service's source
mcq.why: Once repeated use has made a procedure precise and reliably correct, code can run it faster and more consistently than people.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
hook: Your fleet loses a disk every couple of hours. Should each one wake someone up?
title: Don't page a human for every dead disk
body: Good storage alerting pages on two things: user-visible symptoms, such as errors and **SLO burn**, and durability risk, such as data at minimum redundancy or repair falling behind. It does not page on individual disk failures at scale. At about 13 failures a day in a Backblaze-sized fleet, per-disk paging burns people out and buries real problems in noise. Dead disks go to automation and a daily replacement ticket queue.
takeaway: A page should mean a human must act now. Everything else is a ticket.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** 300,000 drives at 1.5 percent AFR is about 4,500 failures a year, about 12 a day. Per-disk pages would be constant noise.

**Why disks don't need humans:** The repair loop rebuilds lost copies automatically, and the physical swap can wait for a routine ticket. What needs a human is automation not coping: many chunks at minimum redundancy, repair falling behind, users seeing errors.

**Alert fatigue is a reliability risk:** Paged a dozen times a day for things that fix themselves, engineers learn to ignore pages, and the one that matters gets missed or delayed.

**Better signal:** Paging on durability risk also catches dangerous combinations, such as a second failure during a rebuild, which a per-disk page would not distinguish from a routine failure.

quiz.q: Two disks die in the same hour. Under per-disk paging, both pages look identical. Under durability-risk alerting, when would this situation page at all?
quiz.a: When the second failure hits data already degraded by the first, leaving chunks at minimum redundancy. Two unrelated failures with healthy margin just go to automation.

mcq.q: What should page a storage on-call engineer?
options: Data at minimum redundancy or repair falling behind
Every individual disk failure in the fleet
Each SMART counter crossing its threshold
Every completed rebuild of a failed disk
mcq.why: Pages should mean a human must act now: durability risk or user-visible symptoms. Routine disk failures go to automation.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
hook: Automation handles hundreds of fleet events a day, and helped cause two famous outages. What should it run?
title: Automation scales operations, and scales disasters
body: At fleet scale most operations must be automated: disk replacement, repair, rebalancing, rolling upgrades, drains. Humans cannot keep up with hundreds of events per day. But automation also causes disasters faster than humans can. The S3 outage in 2017 and the Meta outage in 2021 both involved tools executing destructive operations at scale. Mature teams pair each operation type with a **default mode**, from fully automatic to human-led, and a **guardrail** that limits the damage.
takeaway: Human involvement should rise with how destructive and unfamiliar the operation is.
deeper:
**The mapping:**
1. Single disk failure and repair: fully automatic; rate limits and risk-based priority.
2. Rolling upgrade and firmware: automatic in staged waves; canary analysis, auto-rollback, redundancy budget.
3. Draining a rack: automatic after human approval; verify no sole copies, slow evacuation.
4. Removing a cluster or deleting data: human approval and two-person review; minimum-capacity checks, delay before real deletion.
5. Unknown or novel failure: human-led; runbook and incident process.

**The logic:** Routine, reversible, well-understood operations run without humans, who would only add delay and error. Destructive or novel ones get human judgment, and even then tool guardrails limit what a wrong decision can do.

**No mode without a guardrail:** Even fully automatic operations have limits. Automation without limits is how a small bug or a wrong input becomes a fleet-wide outage in seconds.

quiz.q: One tool can drain racks and delete clusters, and your team wants both fully automatic 'for consistency'. What default mode and guardrail should each get?
quiz.a: Rack drain: automatic after human approval, with sole-copy checks and slow evacuation. Cluster deletion: two-person review, minimum-capacity checks and a delay before real deletion.

mcq.q: Which default mode suits removing a cluster or deleting data?
options: Human approval with two-person review
Fully automatic with rate limits
Automatic in staged waves with canaries
Human-led with only a runbook
mcq.why: Deletion and cluster removal are destructive and irreversible, so they need two-person review plus minimum-capacity checks and a deletion delay.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
hook: Some operations should run fast and unattended, others deliberately slow. What decides which is which?
title: Automate the reversible fast; make the irreversible slow
body: Automation may do anything that is **reversible**, quickly. Anything irreversible should be slow, guarded and ideally reviewed. Deleting data, removing capacity below a threshold and changing placement rules for durability are in the irreversible class. The decision flow asks one question of every event or change: is it reversible and well understood? If yes, automation executes with rate limits. If no, it needs human approval, tool guardrails, and slow execution staged by cell.
takeaway: Slowness is a safety feature when there's no undo button.
deeper:
**Both paths end in monitoring:** Automated or human-approved, every operation is watched against SLOs and durability signals, and any anomaly triggers pause and roll back. Even reversible operations are not fire-and-forget.

**Why the split works:** A reversible mistake can be undone, so its cost is bounded and speed is valuable. An irreversible mistake cannot, so the only protection is catching it before it completes. Slow execution gives monitoring and humans time to stop it partway.

**The placement puzzle:** The rule itself can be changed back. But a placement change moves data, and a wrong one can leave data under-protected. If failures land during that window, the resulting loss cannot be reversed. What matters is whether the consequences are reversible, not whether the config is.

quiz.q: Two operations: rebalancing shards across healthy nodes, and deleting a decommissioned cluster's data. Which gets fast automation and which gets slow, reviewed execution?
quiz.a: Rebalancing is reversible and well understood, so automate it with rate limits. Deletion is irreversible: human approval, guardrails, and slow, staged execution.

mcq.q: Why is slowness itself a safety mechanism for irreversible operations?
options: It gives time to catch and stop a mistake partway
It lowers the load the operation puts on disks
It lets automation skip human review safely
It makes the operation reversible after the fact
mcq.why: An irreversible result can't be undone, so the only protection is noticing and halting before it completes.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
hook: Your ops tool works perfectly with the right input. Which question matters more before you ship it?
title: Ask every tool: what's the worst a wrong input can do?
body: Ask of every operational tool: 'What is the worst thing this command can do if the input is wrong?' If the answer is 'remove a region's capacity' or 'delete a cluster's data', the tool needs three things. A **hard ceiling** on how much it can affect. A **slow mode**, so damage accumulates gradually instead of instantly. And a **second check** before it proceeds. The S3 2017 remediation, remove capacity slowly and never below minimum, is a template worth copying.
takeaway: Design for the typo, the wrong cluster name, and the extra zero.
deeper:
**Intended use versus worst misuse:** Most tools are designed and tested for correct input. The S3 outage happened because an input was wrong, and the tool faithfully did what it was told at full speed.

**What each safeguard covers:**
1. The hard ceiling bounds the maximum damage, whatever the input says.
2. The slow mode means that even within the ceiling, damage unfolds over time, so monitoring and humans can step in.
3. The second check, another engineer's review or an automated invariant validator, catches the wrong input before execution.

**Check the checker:** In the Meta 2021 outage, the audit tool meant to be that second check had a bug, and it failed to stop the maintenance command. Safety checks need testing like everything else.

quiz.q: You're reviewing a new 'drain-cluster' command. It takes a cluster name and drains it at full speed with no confirmation. Which three changes do you request?
quiz.a: A hard ceiling on how much capacity one run can remove, a slow mode so damage unfolds gradually, and a second check, human review or an automated validator, before it proceeds.

mcq.q: What did the Meta 2021 outage add to the 'worst wrong input' lesson?
options: The audit tool meant to block it had a bug
The tool removed capacity faster than allowed
The command ran without any audit tool at all
The wrong input came from an automated script
mcq.why: A maintenance command took down the backbone and a bug in the audit tool failed to stop it, so safety checks need testing too.

section: Key takeaways
hook: Disks fail daily, upgrades outnumber failures 1,000 to 1, and changes cause most outages. How do you cope?
title: Change safely, forever: operations in one card
body: Storage never stops changing: Meta found upgrades about 1,000 times more frequent than failures, and Google says most incidents come from pushes. Repair must be fast, risk-prioritized and widely spread; erasure coding multiplies its traffic. SMART cannot predict most failures. Zero-downtime upgrades need two-way compatibility, graceful handoff and a redundancy budget. **Canaries** detect, **cells** contain, and config gets the same pipeline as code. Migrations need an abstraction layer, dual writes, verification, gradual cutover and rollback.
takeaway: Make every change reversible, contained and observed. Make the rest slow.
deeper:
**Schema changes:** Online schema change tools such as pt-osc, gh-ost and Vitess copy into a ghost table, capture changes, throttle and cut over. Application changes use expand and contract.

**Migrations:** Abstraction layer, dual write, backfill, verify with shadow reads, shift reads gradually, flip the source of truth, keep a rollback window, decommission. Uber, Dropbox, Meta, Discord, GitHub and LinkedIn share the same lessons: long validation, small cutover units, a real rollback path.

**Observability:** Watch durability directly, meaning data at minimum redundancy and repair rate, and use latency histograms, not averages. Google found over 36 percent of failed drives showed no SMART signal at all, so redundancy and repair, not prediction, are the foundation.

**The rule under everything:** Automate reversible operations fully. Make irreversible ones, like deleting data or removing capacity, slow, guarded and reviewed.

quiz.q: A new storage team asks for one principle to judge every operational change by. What do you give them, and what does it look like in practice?
quiz.a: Every change should be reversible, contained and observed: staged rollout, cells, canaries, rollback paths. Anything irreversible, like deletion, must be slow, guarded and reviewed.

mcq.q: Which statement matches the evidence on SMART and drive failure?
options: Over 36% of failed drives showed no SMART signal
SMART predicts most failures a week in advance
Only hot drives failed without SMART warnings
SMART signals become reliable as drives age
mcq.why: Google's 2007 study found over 36% of failed drives had zero SMART counts, so redundancy and repair must carry durability.
